findings.title: Options object enables rejectOnClear by default despite the documented false default
findings.cause: When pLimit receives an options object, line 7 destructures rejectOnClear with a default of true. The documented and typed default is false, so pLimit({concurrency: 1}) now behaves differently from pLimit(1).
findings.impact: Callers who adopt the documented options-object form can unexpectedly reject queued work when clearQueue() is called. In production teardown paths this turns formerly discarded/unsettled pending promises into AbortError rejections, causing Promise.all or await chains to fail unless every pending task has explicit rejection handling.
findings.evidence: index.js:7 sets `{concurrency, rejectOnClear = true}` and clearQueue rejects queued entries at index.js:84-87. readme.md documents `rejectOnClear` default as false and says pending promises are rejected only when rejectOnClear is enabled. Runtime probe with pLimit({concurrency:1}) printed `rejected:AbortError`; the same probe with explicit rejectOnClear:false printed `pending`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import {setTimeout as delay} from 'node:timers/promises'; import pLimit from './index.js'; const limit = pLimit({concurrency:1}); const running = limit(() => delay(50)); const pending = limit(() => delay(1)); await Promise.resolve(); limit.clearQueue(); const state = await Promise.race([pending.then(() => 'fulfilled', error => 'rejected:' + error.name), delay(20).then(() => 'pending')]); await running; console.log(state);" # observed: rejected:AbortError; expected default behavior: pending/discarded unless rejectOnClear:true is supplied

findings.title: Falsey non-boolean rejectOnClear values bypass runtime validation
findings.cause: The validation guard at line 12 checks `rejectOnClear && typeof rejectOnClear !== 'boolean'`, so falsey non-booleans skip the TypeError path even though the API only accepts booleans.
findings.impact: Misconfigured runtime callers can pass values such as 0, an empty string, or null without being told the option is invalid. The value is then silently coerced by clearQueue behavior, hiding configuration bugs and diverging from the TypeScript contract.
findings.evidence: index.js:12 only validates truthy values. index.d.ts declares `readonly rejectOnClear?: boolean`, and readme.md lists Type: boolean. Runtime probe printed `0:accepted`, `"":accepted`, and `null:accepted`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; for (const value of [0, '', null]) { try { pLimit({concurrency:1, rejectOnClear:value}); console.log(JSON.stringify(value)+':accepted'); } catch (error) { console.log(JSON.stringify(value)+':threw:' + error.name); } }"

findings.title: limitFunction drops all caller arguments before invoking the wrapped function
findings.cause: The returned wrapper at line 124 is `() => limit(() => function_())`, so it accepts no rest arguments and always calls the original function without the caller-provided parameters.
findings.impact: Any consumer using limitFunction around a parameterized async function receives undefined arguments, producing wrong results or failed requests while still respecting concurrency. This breaks the generic call signature declared in index.d.ts and covered by index.test-d.ts.
findings.evidence: index.js:124 ignores arguments. index.d.ts exports `limitFunction<Arguments extends unknown[], ReturnType>(function_: (...arguments_: Arguments) => PromiseLike<ReturnType>, ...): (...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>`, and index.test-d.ts calls the returned function as `lf('input')`. Runtime probe printed `undefined:undefined` for a two-argument wrapper called with `left`, `right`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import {limitFunction} from './index.js'; const limited = limitFunction(async (a, b) => String(a)+':'+String(b), {concurrency:1}); console.log(await limited('left','right'));" # observed: undefined:undefined; expected: left:right

findings.title: limit.map passes undefined index for non-array iterables
findings.cause: The mapper call at lines 108-111 checks Array.isArray(iterable) and passes the index only for arrays; Set, iterator, and generator inputs receive undefined for the index parameter.
findings.impact: The public contract says map accepts any iterable and the mapper receives both value and index. Consumers processing Sets, iterator results, or generators with index-dependent logic get undefined indexes, while arrays continue to work, making the bug easy to miss in tests that only assert mapped values.
findings.evidence: readme.md:78-84 and index.d.ts:30-42 state that map accepts an iterable and the mapper receives the item value and index, equivalent to Array.from(iterable, (item, index) => limit(mapperFunction, item, index)). Current index.js:111 passes `iterableIsArray ? index : undefined`. Runtime probe printed `[null,null,null]` for both Set and array iterator inputs because JSON.stringify converts undefined array entries to null; a control probe with an array printed `[0,1,2]`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; const limit = pLimit(2); console.log(JSON.stringify(await limit.map(new Set(['a','b','c']), (_value, index) => index))); console.log(JSON.stringify(await limit.map(['a','b','c'].values(), (_value, index) => index)));" # observed [null,null,null] twice; expected [0,1,2]

findings.title: validateConcurrency rejects Infinity although the previous implementation allowed it
findings.cause: The current validation at line 128 requires Number.isInteger(concurrency), removing the previous `concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` allowance visible in HEAD:index.js.
findings.impact: Users who use pLimit(Infinity) as a no-limit/switchable-concurrency sentinel now get a TypeError during construction instead of a limiter that starts all queued work. This is a compatibility regression for existing runtime callers, although the README only states `number` with minimum 1 and does not explicitly call out Infinity.
findings.evidence: Current index.js:128 rejects any non-integer. `git show HEAD:index.js` shows the prior validator accepted `(Number.isInteger(concurrency) || concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY) && concurrency > 0`. Runtime probe printed `threw:TypeError:Expected `concurrency` to be a number from 1 and up` for pLimit(Infinity).
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; try { const limit = pLimit(Infinity); console.log('accepted', typeof limit); } catch (error) { console.log('threw:' + error.name + ':' + error.message); }"

commands_run: find node_modules -maxdepth 2 -type d -name xo -o -name ava -o -name tsd | sed -n '1,80p'
rg -n "Infinity|rejectOnClear|limitFunction|map accepts|map passes|iterable|index" readme.md test.js index.d.ts index.test-d.ts index.js
agent_testimony: Direct Mode followed: no m1nd tools and no m1nd helper scripts were used. I did not patch the audited repo. npm test could not run because the workspace lacked node_modules/.bin/xo, so I used focused Node runtime probes against the checked-out index.js plus source/documentation/type inspection.
notes: The audited repo was already dirty with modifications to index.js. Findings are based on the current lane workspace contents and source-backed runtime probes. No operator-only artifacts were read.
